clue.text: Large vehicle parking by Irish lake

parts.note: P is the standard abbreviation for parking, as on road signs
a lough is the Irish word for a lake

explanation.surface: A big lorry is left parked beside a lake in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Large vehicle' looks like a lorry; it is the constellation also called Charles's Wain, a wain being a wagon.
explanation.definitionFit: The star group known as Charles's Wain, a great wagon in the sky, is also called by this farm-implement name.

clue.text: Phone up about last of gladioli in bloom

indicators.note: about means the turned-round word goes around the extracted letter
in a down clue, up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: to phone someone is to call them

indicators.note: last of takes only the final letter of the word gladioli

explanation.surface: Someone rings back about the final gladioli flowering.
explanation.definitionFit: A lilac is a flowering shrub, and its blossom is a familiar bloom in gardens.

parts.note: a decorator's first layer of paint is hidden beneath the top coat, so it is seldom on view

explanation.surface: An artist's picture that hardly anyone gets to look at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Painter' suggests an artist and an obscure canvas; it is a house painter, whose base layer is covered over.
explanation.definitionFit: The base layer of paint is applied by a decorator and then covered by the top coat, so nobody sees it.

clue.text: World Cup hero injured netting second

indicators.note: netting means catching inside, so the abbreviation goes within the word for injured

parts.note: injured means hurt

explanation.surface: A football star gets hurt while scoring a second goal.
explanation.walkthrough: Geoff Hurst scored a hat-trick for England in the 1966 World Cup final.
explanation.definitionFit: Geoff Hurst is the English striker celebrated for his hat-trick in the 1966 final, an example of a hero.

clue.text: If in no end of doubt before close of play, declare!

indicators.note: in puts the word If inside the string built from the other pieces
before places the doubt piece ahead of the play piece
end of takes only the last letter of doubt
close of takes only the last letter of play

explanation.surface: A cricket umpire is urged to make a call, free of doubt, before stumps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close of play' suggests cricket stumps but just picks a letter; the surface's 'declare!' is also a cricket term for ending an innings.
explanation.definitionFit: To notify is to announce or make known formally, a synonym of declare as an imperative.

indicators.note: clumsy suggests the letters of Nigel are handled awkwardly and jumbled

parts.note: a chap is a man, a gent

explanation.surface: Nigel, an awkward fellow, is sloppy.
explanation.definitionFit: Being negligent means failing to take proper care, a direct synonym of careless.

indicators.note: first in takes only the opening letter of there

parts.note: to enquire is to ask, so enquires gives asks

explanation.surface: Someone first in line at a counter asks about vacancies.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasks are pieces of work to be done, synonymous with jobs.

parts.note: to restore something is to replace it

explanation.surface: A woman and I are doing up an old hearth.
explanation.definitionFit: The hearth is the floor of the grate where a fire is built, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Not awake when cover pulled up

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

indicators.note: in a down clue, pulled up means the word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: a peel is the outer skin or covering of a fruit

explanation.surface: Someone is jolted awake when the bedclothes are pulled off.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone asleep is in slumber, the opposite state to being awake.

definitions.meaning: to put something down to someone is to attribute or ascribe it
a good reputation or standing, as in a person's honour

explanation.surface: Insulting someone's reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: To credit is to ascribe or attribute; credit also means standing or reputation.

parts.note: so means therefore
a lid is a top on a container

explanation.surface: A logical conclusion that a boss has to be dependable.
explanation.definitionFit: A solid friend or argument is dependable and sound, so the words are synonyms.

clue.text: One who keeps records about substance almost like gold dust

parts.note: re means about or concerning
the gist is the substance or main point

indicators.note: almost means the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: something like gold dust is very scarce, rare

explanation.surface: An archivist deals with something nearly as precious as gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like gold dust' is an idiom for extremely scarce.
explanation.definitionFit: A registrar is an official who keeps registers, such as of births, marriages and deaths.

indicators.note: in puts that letter inside the word for bar

parts.note: bar means except, as in 'all bar one'

indicators.note: primarily takes only the first letter of remarks

explanation.surface: Barbed comments made mainly in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cutting remarks' reads as one phrase; 'Cutting' alone is the definition, a cutting from a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutting, as from a newspaper or book, is an extract or passage taken from it.

clue.text: Trendy little drink I had in flat

parts.note: in means fashionable or trendy
a sip is a small drink
I'd is the contraction of I had

explanation.surface: A fashionable small drink I had in my apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flat' looks like a home; it means dull or tasteless.
explanation.definitionFit: Something insipid is dull and lacking flavour, as a flat drink or performance is.

clue.text: Errand boy committing serious crime in minister's house

indicators.note: committing is read as enclosing, so the crime goes inside the boy

parts.note: a page is a boy who runs errands, as in a hotel
arson, deliberately setting fire, is a serious crime

explanation.surface: A messenger lad commits a grave offence at a vicar's home.
explanation.definitionFit: A parsonage is the house provided for a parish clergyman, a minister of the church.

indicators.note: mostly means the final letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: ice can mean coolness of manner, reserve
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Ice almost surrounds a lake in Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: A reservoir is a large artificial lake used to store water supplies.

clue.text: Creature in a stream grabbing frantic duck

indicators.note: grabbing means the stream word holds the frantic word inside it

parts.note: a rill is a small stream
mad means frantic
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, O

explanation.surface: An animal in a brook seizes a panicking duck.
explanation.definitionFit: The armadillo is an armoured mammal of the Americas, an example of a creature.

clue.text: Be uncomfortably hot right in front of kiln

indicators.note: in front of places the abbreviation ahead of the word for kiln

parts.note: an oast is a kiln for drying hops

explanation.surface: Standing right in front of a furnace, someone swelters.
explanation.definitionFit: To roast, informally, is to be very hot, as in sweltering in the sun.

indicators.note: to divide means the trial word splits the existing word by sitting inside it

parts.note: real means actually existing
a judge hears, that is tries, a case

explanation.surface: Attempts to split up what exists are just a dry run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tries' looks like attempts; it is the legal sense, a court hearing a case.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehearsal is a practice run of a play or performance before the real thing.

parts.note: on means working, as a machine that is on
a set is a group

explanation.surface: A first day at work with a new team.
explanation.definitionFit: The onset of something is its start or beginning, synonymous with opening.

clue.text: Slow on the uptake, but so excited by note, finally

indicators.note: excited suggests the letters of 'but so' stirred up and rearranged
finally takes only the last letter of note

explanation.surface: Someone dim, yet thrilled by a message at last.
explanation.definitionFit: An obtuse person is dull-witted and slow to understand, so slow on the uptake.

clue.text: Contest fewer in number, being without equal

parts.note: a match is a contest or game
less means fewer, a smaller quantity

explanation.surface: A competition with fewer entrants turns out unrivalled.
explanation.definitionFit: Something matchless has no rival or peer, being unequalled.

clue.text: Crime writer tells about that woman topping husband

indicators.note: about means the telling word goes around the shortened pronoun

parts.note: to tell is to say, so tells gives says

indicators.note: topping means removing the top, here the abbreviation for husband at the front

parts.note: her refers to that woman

explanation.surface: A mystery novelist relates how a woman killed her husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topping' looks like killing, fitting a crime story; it means beheading the word, losing H.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorothy L Sayers created the detective Lord Peter Wimsey, so she is a famous crime novelist.

indicators.note: races means runs about wildly, so the letters of Rider at are scrambled

explanation.surface: A jockey at the racecourse is held up.
explanation.definitionFit: To tarry is to linger or be slow in going, so tarried means delayed.

indicators.note: in puts the mirrored word inside it
reflected means the word is mirrored, read backwards

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: A clumsy author sees himself mirrored in a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone inept lacks skill and is clumsy, a synonym of awkward.

clue.text: Gossip present, reportedly with chance to speak

indicators.note: reportedly signals a word heard rather than read, a soundalike

parts.note: present means in attendance, here
to have one's say is to have a chance to speak

explanation.surface: Rumours in attendance, said with the opportunity to talk.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearsay is information passed on from others, rumour rather than fact, i.e. gossip.

definitions.meaning: Thomas ..., author of Tess of the d'Urbervilles

explanation.surface: A portly writer of fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardy means robust and tough; Thomas Hardy was the Victorian novelist of Wessex.

indicators.note: drifting suggests the letters of Slav wander out of order

parts.note: O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: A burst of gunfire from an Eastern European wandering across.
explanation.definitionFit: A salvo is a simultaneous discharge of guns, so a volley.

indicators.note: swimming suggests the letters of over shell float about and rearrange

explanation.surface: A duck paddles past a shell in the water.
explanation.definitionFit: The shoveler, a dabbling duck with a broad spoon-shaped bill, is an example of a duck.

clue.text: Type of energy supply also run

indicators.note: supply is read as the adverb of supple, flexibly, so the letters of also bend into a new order

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Power is also delivered by a scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' looks like a noun for providing; it is the adverb 'in a supple way'.
explanation.definitionFit: Solar power is energy taken from the sun, one type of renewable energy.

indicators.note: crossing means the river letter goes across inside the phrase for reached

parts.note: got to means reached

explanation.surface: Explorers ford a river and arrive at a cavern.
explanation.definitionFit: A grotto is a small picturesque cave, so a cave is a fair synonym.

indicators.note: decapitated means the head, the first letter, is cut off

parts.note: a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A hen in the farmyard has its head chopped off by a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicken and yellow are both informal adjectives for cowardly.
